extracted.intended_audience: NLP/ML researchers, meta-science scholars, and developers building automated peer-review analysis or review-quality assessment tools
extracted.subtask_description: Annotating peer-review texts (ICLR 2018 reviews) at the sentence/phrase level across four layers: paper-section correspondence, paper-aspect category, statement purpose (role), and statement significance, with sentiment labels for some layers. The dataset and guidelines support NLP tasks and evaluation of review quality/exhaustiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Layer 1: Review-Paper Section Correspondence (overall)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify the section of the paper on which the review-statement is commenting (labels are simple and obvious for ML papers; e.g., Methodology, Experiments, Results, Analysis, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Annotators map each review statement to a paper section label from Table 2. Note some labels (MET, EXP, RES, ANA) are inter-linked and can be hard to distinguish. Not all labels are prominent in reviews (e.g., ABS, INT, FWK). Phrase-level annotation is allowed when a sentence comments on multiple sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract (ABS)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the reviewer is explicitly commenting on the Abstract of the paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'The title and abstract are not very reflective of the content of the text.' Use ABS only when reviewer explicitly mentions the abstract.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduction (INT)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the reviewer is explicitly commenting on the Introduction of the paper or provides a general summary at the beginning of the review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'This paper introduces a technique for program synthesis ...' The Overall label may overlap with INT for general comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Related Works (RWK)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the reviewer is talking explicitly about the Literature/Related Work section or comments on some related research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'The general idea of multi-scale generation is not new, and has been investigated for instance in LapGAN ...' Use when reviewer references prior work or literature coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem Definition/Idea (PDI)
rubrics_metrics.description: Review statement that comments on the problem being investigated or the main scientific idea in the paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'The idea behind the paper is novel: translating language modeling into a matrix factorization problem is new as far as I know.' Use when the reviewer addresses the core problem or idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data/Datasets (DAT)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any statement on the data, datasets, or corpus used in the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Also, more monolingual experiments could have been conducted with state-of-the-art neural paraphrasing models on WikiQA and Quora datasets.' Include comments on data choice, preprocessing, availability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodology (MET)
rubrics_metrics.description: Review comments on methods, the approach described in the paper, or details on how the problem has been addressed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Long technical description of the algorithm. MET often overlaps with EXP/RES and can be hard to separate; annotate phrase-level where needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experiments (EXP)
rubrics_metrics.description: Review comments on the experimental section, parameter/hyperparameter details, training/testing configuration, what has been done, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'The experiment section is thorough ... and supports reproducibility.' Include critique of experimental design, baselines, settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Results (RES)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments on the results or outcome of experiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'The paper only shows results on image generation from random noise.' Use when reviewer discusses reported numbers, performance, or empirical findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tables & Figures (TNF)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments explicitly specifying the tables and figures within the paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'The figures in this paper depend excessively and unnecessarily on color.' Use for visual/formatting feedback tied to specific tables/figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analysis (ANA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments on analysis of results or studies on outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'It would be interesting ... to study why they achieve robustness to noise.' Use when reviewer asks for or criticizes deeper analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Future Work (FWK)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments on the future of the work, impact on the community, or directions for extension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'This will give the hardware community a clear vision ...' Use when reviewer comments on possible follow-ups or broader impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall (OAL)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments not confined to a certain section and about the overall work in general (sometimes overlaps with Introduction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Despite these questions ... this paper is a nice addition ... and should be accepted.' Use for holistic judgments or general impressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bibliography (BIB)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any straightforward comments on the references or bibliography section of the paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'I found some references are incomplete and should be expanded.' Use for missing/incorrect citations or related literature coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: External (EXT)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the reviewer brings external knowledge from their expertise to justify a point that cannot be classified into other section-labels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Mujoco + AI Gym should make this really easy to do (for reference, I have no relationship with OpenAI).' Use when reviewer cites outside resources or domain knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Layer 2: Review-Paper Aspect (overall)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify the aspect of the paper the review-statement addresses (aspect-labels are intuitive for empirical ML: novelty, significance, soundness, comparison, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aspect labels are not explicitly commanded by ICLR but an ideal review should address many of them. Annotators can leave instances unlabeled if they don't conform. See appendix/ACL 2016 guidelines for further definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness (APR)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the reviewer comments on the scope of the article to the conference or the suitability/standard of the article to the venue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'This time the paper does not deserve to be published under ICLR.' Use when reviewer judges fit to venue or audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality or Novelty (NOV)
rubrics_metrics.description: Review-comments on the novelty or originality of the submission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'The main novelty ... is the choice of models ...' Use when reviewer assesses how new or inventive the work is.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance or Impact (IMP)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the reviewer comments on the significance of the work (e.g., whether it will inspire ideas or be impactful to the community).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Contains more ideas or results than most publications ... goes the extra mile.' Use for broader community or scientific impact judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaningful Comparison (CMP)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the reviewer comments whether the work is compared against earlier approaches or how it stands against existing literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Bibliography and comparison are somewhat helpful, but it could be hard to determine exactly how this work relates to previous work.' Use for baseline/ablation/related-work adequacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation & Formatting (PNF)
rubrics_metrics.description: Review-comments on presentation and formatting aspects of the paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Section 2, paragraph 3: “is given in Fig 1” -> “is given in Algorithm 1”' Use for editorial, layout, or clarity-of-presentation issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendation (REC)
rubrics_metrics.description: Overall recommendation of the reviewer on the article for inclusion/exclusion from the proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'I strongly recommend this paper for publication.' Use for accept/reject/weak/strong recommendations and summary judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical & Theoretical Soundness (EMP)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the reviewer comments on the soundness of the approach (empirical or theoretical), i.e., whether arguments are cogent and supported.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'The empirical results appear promising ...' Use for correctness, validity, robustness, and reproducibility concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substance (SUB)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the reviewer comments on the volume of work done and whether there is enough substance to warrant publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'I wish the paper had explored a wider variety of dataset tasks ...' Use when reviewer judges scope, breadth, or completeness of contributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity (CLA)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the reviewer comments about writing quality, structure, or whether contributions are clear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'It was easy to read the paper and understand it.' Use when reviewer discusses readability, organization, or explanatory quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Layer 3: Review-Statement Purpose (overall)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify the purpose/role of the peer review statement within the review — uncovers reviewer intent (summary, suggestion, deficit, appreciation, question, criticism, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Table 3 presents labels and examples. Annotation is multi-label to address overlapping roles (e.g., Deficit and Criticism). Some labels are related and may be merged later to avoid ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary (SMY)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provides a summary of the work reflecting the reviewer's understanding, usually at the beginning of the review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'The paper proposes a novel approach ...' Use for concise restatements of aims/methods/results indicating reviewer comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suggestion (SUG)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provides suggestions to the author to improve or include additional details for clarity (e.g., evidence, artifacts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'If the authors would have demonstrated all 8-bit training on all datasets ... this would be more useful.' Use when reviewer offers actionable improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deficit (DFT)
rubrics_metrics.description: Highlights major/minor flaws/shortcomings in the paper, usually confidently stated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'The paper does not explain the HDDA formalism ...' Use for substantive criticisms identifying weaknesses or missing pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appreciation (APC)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applauds the authors about their work, highlighting positive aspects or specific sections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'As adversarial training is an important topic ... I feel this work may lead to promising ...' Use for praise or positive reinforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discussion (DIS)
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements where the reviewer provides explanations or additional insights, usually neutral in polarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Expository sentences clarifying methods or background. Use for neutral elaboration or contextualization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Question (QSN)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewer explicitly poses a question to the authors (often ends with ?), asking for explanation or clarification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Can authors provide some justifications of such different choices of activation functions?' Use when reviewer requests information or clarification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criticism (CRT)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewer is critical of the work, usually highlights a deficit and bears explicit negative sentiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'The motivation for detecting adversarial examples is not stated clearly enough ...' Use when reviewer issues evaluative negative statements distinct from neutral discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feedback (FBK)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewer clearly brings out their view toward the work, usually leading to acceptance/rejection statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'In overall, this paper is an accept since it shows good performance ...' Use when reviewer states judgment or decision-oriented commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Layer 4: Review-Statement Significance (overall)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify the relative importance of the review statement within the peer review: Major (MAJ), Minor (MIN), General (GEN). Purpose is to find crucial statements that aid editor/area chair decision-making and meta-review drafting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Annotate statements that would influence final decisions (MAJ), easily fixable/presentation issues (MIN), or general comments (GEN).

rubrics_metrics.name: Major Comment (MAJ)
rubrics_metrics.description: A strong statement highlighting an opinionated view on a major aspect/section or the entire paper (critical flaw or major appreciation) that the editor/chair should consider in decision-making.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'According to the authors, relevance is one of the three criteria ... however, the proposed neural network architecture does not capture relevance.' Use MAJ for statements that could change accept/reject outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minor Comment (MIN)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments that would not play a decisive role; usually presentation/formatting/missing references and can be quickly addressed by the author.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'There are only mostly minor issues with the algorithm development ...' Use MIN for typos, small clarifications, or easy fixes.

rubrics_metrics.name: General Comment (GEN)
rubrics_metrics.description: Regular comments that could not be classified into MAJ or MIN; usually discussions and non-opinionated statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'The related work section is entirely focused on deep learning, while the experiment section is dedicated to sentiment analysis.' Use GEN for descriptive or neutral commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentiment annotation for Layer 1 & Layer 2 (positive/negative/neutral)
rubrics_metrics.description: Annotate sentiment (positive, negative, neutral) of reviewer statements for the layer 1 (section) and layer 2 (aspect) labels as an indicator of the reviewer's perspective on different sections/aspects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sentiment labels are recorded for layers 1 and 2 because polarity is a useful signal of reviewer stance. Use POS/NEG/NEU examples provided in the paper; sentiment helps quantify reviewer implicit view.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review Exhaustiveness (coverage) as a quality dimension
rubrics_metrics.description: Exhaustiveness measures how much the review covers major sections/aspects and performs definitive roles; an exhaustive review addresses many paper sections and aspects and clearly expresses the reviewer's stance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paper notes length is an important signal but not sufficient alone. Exhaustiveness is operationalized via multi-layer labels (coverage across sections/aspects, roles, and significance). Use coverage of major sections/aspects and presence of major comments as indicators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review Quality (composite criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: A good peer review should comment on important sections, address critical aspects, perform definitive roles (summary, suggestions, criticisms), and clearly convey the reviewer's judgment — these constitute dimensions of review quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors assert these components together indicate review quality; however, domain differences exist (e.g., humanities may focus deeply on few points). The dataset supports computational proxies for quality via the annotated layers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annotation multi-label policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Annotators may assign multiple labels to a single statement because labels can overlap in scope (e.g., Deficit vs Criticism; INT vs OAL).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The annotation is intentionally multi-label to handle overlap. The authors plan to merge some labels in future iterations to reduce ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phrase-level annotation guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: When a compound sentence contains comments about different aspects/sections with different sentiment polarity, annotators should perform phrase-level annotation rather than coarse sentence-level labeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: If a sentence comments on two different aspects with different polarities, split and annotate each phrase separately. This improves granularity and correctness of labels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leave unlabeled when no aspect fits
rubrics_metrics.description: Annotators are instructed to leave instances unlabeled if a review sentence does not conform to the prescribed aspect labels (per ACL 2016 reviewing guidelines).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some review sentences may not match any aspect-labels; annotators should skip labeling in such cases rather than force-fitting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Five NLP tasks defined on the dataset
rubrics_metrics.description: Five tasks to probe peer-review analysis and review exhaustiveness: Review Paper Section Correspondence, Paper Aspect Category Detection, Review Statement Role Prediction, Review Statement Significance Detection, and Meta-Review Generation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tasks are intended as benchmarks; baseline experiments (e.g., BERT) were run, results reported. Task 5 (meta-review generation) was particularly challenging with poorer baseline performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of dataset for estimating which comments influence decision (significance signals)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify comments that are central to the review and influence the overall decision (major vs minor vs general) to help area chairs and to estimate reviewer confidence/strength.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Label significance (MAJ/MIN/GEN) and role labels assist in computationally extracting crucial statements usable for meta-review drafting or highlighting high-impact reviewer comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annotation provenance & dataset composition requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Dataset should include metadata: source platform (OpenReview), paper decision class (Accepted/Rejected/Withdrawn), and sentence-level counts to support fair study across classes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors collected reviews from ACC/REJ/WDR to avoid bias; table 1 shows statistics (1199 reviews, ~17k sentences). When applying schema to other domains, account for domain-specific review styles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domain-adaptivity caveat (discipline differences)
rubrics_metrics.description: Annotations and assumptions (e.g., exhaustiveness as good) can be domain-specific; e.g., humanities/social sciences reviews may focus in depth on few sections rather than covering many sections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Annotators/analysts should be cautious applying ML-trained models or metrics across disciplines without adjusting for differences in review norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guidance on ambiguous/inter-linked labels
rubrics_metrics.description: Some labels are inter-linked and hard to distinguish (e.g., MET vs EXP vs RES; DFT vs CRT); annotation guidelines acknowledge fuzziness and allow multi-labeling and future merging.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Annotators should rely on examples in Tables 2 and 3, use phrase-level splits where necessary, and accept overlap. The authors recommend community-driven refinement of the ontology in future iterations.
